vignette:
He is a 36-year-old South Asian man who now works as a detective, a role that suits the parts of him that are methodical, observant, and determined to keep moving forward. In session, he describes his childhood as something he survived rather than something he lived through. He grew up in a home where fear was ordinary and unpredictable. His caregiver, the person who was supposed to protect him, was instead the source of repeated physical abuse. He remembers learning early how to read footsteps in the hallway, the tone of a voice, the way a door shut, because those small things could tell him whether he needed to hide, stay silent, or brace himself. He says that as a boy he became “very good at disappearing while still being in the room.”

The abuse begins when he is young and continues over years, shaping the way he sees himself and other people. He does not describe dramatic single moments so much as a long chain of dread. He remembers the body as the place where the fear lives: shoulders up around his ears, stomach tight, jaw clenched so hard it aches. When he is struck, he learns to go still, to make himself smaller, to accept pain without crying because crying only seems to prolong it. Even now he speaks about those years with a flatness that feels like practice, as if he learned long ago that emotion was unsafe or useless. He carries a deep belief that he should have been stronger, smarter, or more deserving of kindness, and this belief has not entirely loosened with age.

As an adult, he leaves home and builds a life that looks stable from the outside. He marries a woman he trusts, and he describes her as patient in a way that sometimes unsettles him because he is not used to patience arriving without a price. He becomes a detective, drawn partly to structure and partly to the sense that he can impose order on disorder. The job also keeps him close to danger in a way that feels familiar. He is competent, attentive, and often praised for noticing details others miss. At the same time, he is hypervigilant in ways that extend beyond work. He scans rooms automatically, positions himself near exits, and is quick to identify threat. In the field, these habits can make him effective; at home, they leave him restless and unable to settle even when nothing is wrong.

The trauma does not stay in the past. It intrudes through sleep first. He has nightmares that are not always exact replayings of events, but they carry the same helplessness. He wakes tense and disoriented, sometimes reaching for his wife without fully knowing why. Certain sounds—raised voices, footsteps moving quickly down a hall, a belt buckle hitting a chair, even the sharp clap of a hand against a table—can send a jolt through him. He does not always react outwardly. More often, he goes quiet, his mind racing while his face stays controlled. He notices this in the detective work too: interviews with angry suspects can leave him feeling as though he has been flung back into a smaller, more dangerous body. Afterwards he may sit in his car before driving home, gripping the steering wheel and waiting for his breathing to slow.

He avoids talking about the abuse with most people, including much of his family. He says that once he starts, the memories come in pieces and he loses track of where he is. There are gaps in how he remembers his childhood, but some fragments are vivid: the smell of alcohol on a caregiver’s breath, the coldness of tile under his knees, the humiliation of being told he was weak. He feels shame that is hard to name and harder to shake. Although he is now married and outwardly steady, he still struggles with closeness when he feels cornered or criticized. In those moments he can become abruptly distant, not because he wants to push his wife away, but because some part of him expects that intimacy will turn dangerous.

He presents as a man who has spent years functioning at a high level while carrying an internal alarm that rarely shuts off. He is proud of being reliable, and he rarely allows himself to be cared for without discomfort. Underneath that competence is a persistent sense of being on guard, as if the world could turn hostile at any moment. He knows how to read threats, how to endure pain, how to keep working while carrying fear in silence. More recently, he has begun to notice how much effort it takes to keep his life organized around control, and how exhausting it is to remain prepared for harm that is no longer supposed to be waiting for him.
